item.title: North Korean Hackers May Have Stolen Billions. It Wouldn’t Be Their First Heist.
item.description:
Poor, isolated and heavily sanctioned, North Korea is not a country you would expect to field an elite army of hackers capable of pulling off billion-dollar heists.

But for years, security officials had warned that the regime’s cyberattacks were becoming increasingly sophisticated, looting enormous sums to support North Korea’s military and nuclear weapons program.

Those fears peaked this week when Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said that hackers had made off with some $6 billion in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history. Crypto research firms quickly attributed the attack to North Korea, saying it bore the hallmarks of the country’s previous hacks — although officials have not confirmed the North’s role.

Powered by a pipeline of top-class programming students, North Korea’s hacking units have penetrated banks and companies and capitalized on the rise of crypto. A U.N. panel in 2024 found the regime’s cyberattacks had generated about half its foreign currency income, amounting to billions in revenue. Experts agree that the regime is now one of the biggest and most capable cyber threats in the world.

As investigators dig into the Binance attack, here is a look at some of the most famous North Korean hacks.

In 2014, the tech and media giant Sony Pictures was preparing to release “The Interview,” a far-fetched comedy about the assassination of the North’s leader.

Then, American officials said, hackers associated with the Lazarus Group, a shadowy hacking syndicate backed by the North Korean government, breached the company’s computers.

The attacks caused the leaks of internal documents containing salary information that humiliated top company officials and stole terabytes of data.

North Korea has never formally taken responsibility for the attack. At the time, however, Kim Jong-un, the country’s dictator, called the film an “act of terrorism.”

In 2016, North Korean hackers tried to steal about $1 billion from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Only a spelling error stopped them.

Using a payment messaging system known as SWIFT, the hackers were able to persuade the New York Fed to move money to accounts in the Philippines. The hackers were looting an account of the Bangladesh Central Bank when bankers grew suspicious about a withdrawal request that had misspelled “foundation” as “fandation.”

Still, the hackers made off with $81 million from the central bank of Bangladesh.

The attack was important because it showed how savvy North Korean hackers were becoming. In contrast to off-the-shelf tools that had been used in other attacks at the time, the malware the thieves devised for this heist was a custom code, configured for a specific bank. Written from scratch, it was unfamiliar to existing virus-protection programs.

As the cryptocurrency market boomed in the mid 2010s, North Korea began targeting firms in the industry, escalating to large-scale attacks on crypto exchanges by 2020, according to a North Korea-focused publication of the Stimson Center, a Washington-based think tank.

North Korean hackers were accused of stealing $571 million from crypto exchanges between January 2017 and September 2018 and $316 million from 2019 to November 2020.

With borders shut because of the coronavirus pandemic and traditional banks strengthening their firewalls against hackers, cryptocurrency theft was becoming an increasingly vital source of foreign currency for the regime.

In 2022, the United States publicly accused the Lazarus Group of stealing $620 million in cryptocurrency from the video game Axie Infinity.

That year, North Korea’s haul was a little under $1 billion, according to Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, which found 50 percent of the industry’s yearly losses were from North Korean hacks.

Given the history of spectacular market crashes, crypto is hardly a stable source of funding. But at a time when North Korea had locked itself down during the pandemic, hacking crypto exchanges allowed it to generate income in ways that were both Covid-safe and harder to trace in an industry subject to limited government oversight.

In February 2025, North Korean hackers pulled off what was then the biggest heist in the crypto industry’s history, stealing $1.5 billion in cryptocurrencies, according to the F.B.I.

To pull off the breach, the hackers exploited the cryptocurrency exchange ByBit’s reliance on a free software product.

The North Korean hackers had tricked the chief executive of Bybit, Ben Zhou, into authorizing a seemingly routine transaction that handed them control of the exchange’s system.

After looting Bybit, the North Korean hackers spread the stolen funds across a vast web of online crypto wallets, a money-laundering strategy that they had also employed after other heists.

This week, that record was broken in the Binance hack. Hackers stole $6.3 billion in an attack that used “laundering patterns we have not seen before,” Chainalysis wrote in a blog post on Friday.

Binance initially said that the hackers might have compromised an engineer’s laptop, leading to unauthorized withdrawals. But in an update on social media on Friday, the company said it had identified “additional points of breach.”

The specifics of the attack are still being established. TRM Labs, a crypto research firm, said it appeared to be the work of TraderTraitor, which the F.B.I. says is another name for the Lazarus Group.

But U.S. officials have not yet publicly attributed the hack to North Korea.

item.title: Do Animals Grieve?
item.description:
Loren Elliott for The New York Times

Supported by

The feeling of existential loss was long thought to be uniquely human. But studies of coyotes, cockatoos and other creatures are prompting some scientists to reconsider.

By Emily Anthes

Coyotes are not obvious romantics. Their habit of stalking across the landscape alone has earned them a reputation as solitary creatures — and not particularly popular ones, with a public image that ranges from troublesome nuisance to dangerous predator.

But they are deeply loyal mates. They remain with their partners for life, grooming each other, sharing food and raising pups together. “Basically, until death do us part,” said Sara Freeman, a neuroscientist at Utah State University.

In her airy, third-floor laboratory, Dr. Freeman is trying to understand how coyote couples forge these bonds — and what happens when they are broken.

“This is a widowed brain,” she said, pulling a few foil-wrapped packages from an ultracold freezer one morning in August. Each held a block of brain tissue, collected from a female coyote who had outlived her mate.

A student began shaving the frozen tissue into paper-thin slices, using the tip of a small paintbrush to nudge each translucent cross-section onto a glass slide. Later, the researchers would examine the samples, looking for neurological signs of “what we would call a grief state,” Dr. Freeman said.

The study remains in early stages, and it could take years to find clear answers. But the project is one of many in the young field of comparative thanatology, an interdisciplinary effort to unpack how animals respond to — and what they might understand about — death.

Evocative anecdotes abound. In 1972, Jane Goodall watched as a chimp named Flint stopped eating and socializing after the death of his mother, Flo; he died, weeks later, near the spot where her body had once lain. In 2003, African elephants were seen repeatedly returning to the body of a fallen matriarch, periodically prodding her with their trunks. In 2018, an orca named Tahlequah spent at least 17 days swimming with the body of her dead calf.

But whether animals experience grief — a complex, often long-lasting psychological and biological response to loss — remains an open question. “It’s definitely one of those great mysteries,” said Jennifer Vonk, a comparative cognitive psychologist at Oakland University. “And a challenge for scientists.”

Animal deaths are often unpredictable and unseen, especially in the wild. And grief is a complex and loaded concept; it’s easy to project our human experiences onto other creatures and impossible to truly get inside their heads.

Scientists are trying anyway. “The field is ripe for development,” said André Gonçalves, a comparative cognitive scientist at the Indianapolis Zoological Society. “I mean, mortality is kind of a big deal, right?”

For decades, many scientists maintained that grief was unique to humans. Researchers who dared to suggest otherwise, armed with anecdotes about animals like Flint, were accused of committing the sin of anthropomorphism — viewing animals through a human-centered lens — and of venturing beyond the available data.

In 2008, an elderly chimpanzee named Pansy unwittingly provided compelling new data. When she died at a British wildlife park, two overhead cameras captured the reactions of her three chimpanzee companions. In the minutes before Pansy died, the other chimps gently groomed and caressed her.

After Pansy took her last breaths, her daughter spent hours beside her body. The other adult female spent an unusually long time grooming her own son. All three chimps slept fitfully that night. And when they awoke, they picked some stray bits of straw from Pansy’s body, then watched quietly as keepers carried her away.

“The chimpanzees seemed to know that this was a momentous event,” said James Anderson, a primatologist at Kyoto University.

In 2010, Dr. Anderson and his colleagues published a detailed analysis of the footage, noting that the behaviors of the surviving chimps were “strikingly reminiscent of human responses to peaceful death.”

“We propose that chimpanzees’ awareness of death has been underestimated,” they added.

The Pansy paper seemed to embolden other researchers to write up their own observations of animal responses to death. Soon, scientists were designing new research projects and looking for patterns in the growing pile of case studies.

“It kind of started snowballing,” said Susana Monsó, a philosopher of animal minds at the National University of Distance Education in Madrid and the author of “Playing Possum: How Animals Understand Death.”

There is no magic formula for determining whether an animal’s behavior qualifies as grief, said Barbara J. King, an anthropologist at William & Mary and the author of “How Animals Grieve.” But changes in daily routines and “species-specific signals of deep sorrow” are among the indicators that animals might be in mourning, Dr. King said.

Many studies document behaviors that seem to fit the bill. Apes, monkeys, dolphins and whales sometimes carry the corpses of their young for days or weeks. Some bereaved macaque mothers become isolated and withdrawn, receiving less grooming and initiating fewer hugs. Giraffes stand vigil over fallen calves; elephants touch the bones of their dead. Dogs, cats and horses sometimes seem to lose interest in food after the death of animal (or human) companions, owners have reported.

Whether these behaviors are signs of sorrow is open to interpretation, and reports from animal caretakers are not always reliable. (Bereaved pet owners might project their own grief onto their surviving animals.) But to Dr. King, there are more than enough credible reports to be convincing. “Grief is not a ‘human’ behavior, by which I mean it’s not a human-only behavior,” she said.

Other scientists are more circumspect. “I would really like there to be strong evidence of grief,” said Alecia Carter, an evolutionary anthropologist at University College London. “But I just personally haven’t found very much.”

Even a behavior like clinging to a corpse is not necessarily easy to interpret. In a 2021 meta-analysis, Dr. Carter and her colleagues found that primate mothers were more likely to carry infants who had died from “nontraumatic” causes, like disease, than from accidents or attacks, which often leave more obvious injuries. The behavior was also more common among young mothers than older ones.

One possible explanation? Primate mothers are most likely to carry dead infants when they don’t fully recognize that they are dead. That’s just a hypothesis, and even Dr. Carter doesn’t find it to be entirely convincing. But it highlights the need to be cautious when drawing conclusions about what’s driving animal behavior.

While anthropologists and zoologists document animal behavior, neuroscientists are peering into the brain. Many are focused on monogamous species that form strong pair bonds, like prairie voles and California mice, simulating death by permanently separating animals from their mates.

This kind of romantic rupture can produce signs of anxiety and what scientists call behavioral despair. After losing their partners, male prairie voles are quicker to abandon their attempts to escape from cylinders full of water, for example. Such losses also activate the brain’s stress circuits and disrupts the signaling pathways for oxytocin, a hormone that facilitates bonding. In a small early analysis of three widowed coyotes, Dr. Freeman of Utah State found that changes to the brain’s stress pathways might begin within days and last for over a year.

Breaking individual bonds can have effects distinct from those of general isolation. One recent study found that after losing a mate, California mice showed signs of heightened brain inflammation. Un-bonded mice housed alone did not.

“An animal that has never had a partner is biologically different from an animal that had a partner and lost their relationship,” said Erica Glasper, a behavioral neuroscientist at Ohio State University who led the research.

Some of these findings have tantalizing parallels in humans. For example, losing a spouse seems to promote inflammation in people, an effect that becomes more pronounced as grief severity increases.

Still, Dr. Glasper is reluctant to say that the mice are in mourning. “Our data tell us that the loss does matter to the animal,” she said. “It can’t really tell us how they feel. We can’t ask the mouse whether it’s longing for its partner.”

That’s a critical question, said Zoe Donaldson, a behavioral neuroscientist at the University of Colorado Boulder. “Yearning is what differentiates grief from depression,” she said.

Some emerging research, from Dr. Donaldson and others, suggests that voles might yearn for missing mates. Dopamine, which plays a crucial role in motivation, seems to drive a vole’s desire for its partner. The hormone spikes when voles are seeking out their mates or anticipating reuniting with them. And several studies suggest that a five- to seven-day separation may increase a vole’s to reunite with its partner and amplify dopamine signaling in the brain.

Dr. Donaldson, who said she had initially been dismissive of the idea that the monogamous rodents could mourn, now believes that prairie voles experience “something akin to grief.”

While scientists tend to be cautious, the public has embraced the idea of animal grief. In a survey of 1,000 Australian adults, 90 percent said that some animals could grieve and 23 percent said that all of them could. Among those who believed that animals could mourn, 18 percent attributed grief to ants; 10 percent to prawns.

“People have incredibly intense emotions around this when I talk about my research,” Dr. Donaldson said. “Like, ‘I can’t believe you’re taking away their partners.’”

Animals don’t need to understand abstract concepts like nonexistence in order to know something important about death, some experts argue.

Dr. Monsó, the philosopher of animal minds, has outlined a “minimal concept of death,” which requires understanding just two essential concepts: nonfunctionality, or the idea that dead animals don’t do things that living ones do, and irreversibility, “which is the idea that unlike asleep individuals, dead individuals don’t go back to doing things,” she said.

In a new study, Dr. Monsó and her colleagues found that Goffin’s cockatoos, brainy birds that are known to be talented tool users, could distinguish between permanently broken, or “dead,” tools and those that were only temporarily out of commission.

The findings suggest that the birds may have “some of the cognitive prerequisites” for understanding death, Dr. Monsó said. But even if they don’t, she added, animals don’t necessarily need to understand death in order to feel grief.

Dr. Gonçalves of the Indianapolis Zoological Society agreed. Three-year-olds don’t fully comprehend death, he noted, but few people would question whether they’re capable of mourning a dead parent. “We readily attribute them with grief,” he said.

In some ways, the debate over animal grief has become a semantic one. The loss of a close companion can cause emotional distress in animals, scientists agreed. At issue was whether that distress could be called grief.

“There’s part of me, as an animal behaviorist, that definitely hesitates a little bit,” Dr. Freeman said. “You can’t just say animals grieve and then not stand behind it with data.”

But there’s plenty of reason to believe that animals can mourn, she said, and as the data come in, she would rather err in the direction of assuming that their sorrow is real: “It offers the opportunity to give them credit, perhaps, for a richer lived experience than we often ascribe to wild animals.”

Anecdotes have their limits, but they also have real power — and they’ve played a huge role in opening our minds to the reality of animal grief. So what have you seen in your own lives, whether it's a pet responding to the loss of a companion or an encounter in the wild? Let’s add to the growing list of observations.

item.title: Are Freezers Being Hacked? Europe and the U.S. Military Are Investigating.
item.description:
A spate of appliance malfunctions at U.S. military facilities over the summer seemed like just a nuisance: Refrigeration systems had failed at commissaries, spoiling food and temporarily limiting supplies.

Then, last month, freezers malfunctioned at hundreds of grocery stores in France in what officials called a cyberattack. On Monday, retailers in at least seven more European countries reported problems with refrigeration units.

Though it was not clear what caused the disruptions, experts said they had the hallmarks of cyberattacks. On Monday, the U.S. Army said that its cyber investigators were looking into the issue.

Here’s what to know:

On Aug. 26, freezers at a market in Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona, suddenly went into defrost mode, according to a Facebook post from the base. All the food in those freezers was spoiled.

The same day, Naval Station Newport in Newport, R.I., reported “refrigeration system issues at the commissary.”

Army officials are now investigating whether those malfunctions and others at U.S. military facilities in August were part of a wider cyberattack, Reuters reported last week. Asked on Monday about the Reuters report, the Pentagon acknowledged “speculation regarding a potential cyber incident” and said that its inspector general’s office was investigating the matter.

The Army’s Criminal Investigative Division separately confirmed that its Cyber Field Office was looking into what happened at the commissaries — and working with French law enforcement agencies “in understanding the refrigeration outages in Europe.”

Last month, hundreds of supermarket refrigeration systems were targeted in France, with more than 400 stores experiencing some form of equipment malfunction. The French authorities said they were investigating it as a cyberattack, but have not identified culprits.

On Monday, supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported issues with cooling systems. Many of the stores reported that the temperature in the units started rising uncontrollably, blowing hot air and spoiling the refrigerated products.

Brecht Stinkens, 38, manager of a Delhaize supermarket in Hoeilaart, Belgium, said in an interview that alarms were going off on several of his refrigerators at 4 a.m. Monday, and he immediately thought of what happened in France.

“Given what happened 14 days ago, I already knew what was going on,” he said. He estimated that his store lost about 100,000 euros ($112,000) because of spoiled food.

No one has claimed responsibility. The federal prosecutor’s office in Belgium said that it had opened an investigation into the malfunctions, though it did not say they were the result of a cyberattack.

The European Commission issued a statement that suggested it believed the systems had been hacked. It showed how “cyberattacks can disrupt services, affect businesses and directly affect citizens’ daily lives,” said Louise Bogey, a spokeswoman for the commission, the European Union’s executive arm.

Yes. Many supermarkets and large chains use centrally connected refrigeration systems with temperatures that are set remotely using internet connections. While many of these systems have cybersecurity protections, older ones are more vulnerable to hackers.

“We have a huge legacy problem in food and beverage as a whole,” said Sean Tufts, the chief technology officer of Claroty, a cybersecurity company in New York. “Historically, those kinds of things were always offline.”

The attack in France last month targeted systems made by three manufacturers whose units were remotely controlled, the national cybersecurity agency said at the time. Danfoss, one of the manufacturers, said that most of the affected units were older and did not have software updates that many manufacturers now use to secure their systems.

Mr. Stinkens said that the monitoring equipment for his store’s cooling system was also supplied by Danfoss. “That system was hacked,” he said.

The glitches highlight what experts say is the vulnerability of supply chains for day-to-day goods, especially as more parts of the consumer economy are connected to the internet.

Banks and technology companies have spent years building systems to protect against these sorts of weaknesses, but it is only more recently that workaday appliances such as freezers have become targets, experts said. For malicious actors, panic can be sowed by disrupting something as common as a grocery store, Mr. Tufts said.

“Food security is often taken for granted in Western countries,” said Richard Jones, a professor of criminology at the University of Edinburgh who studies cybersecurity and supply chains. “This is a wake-up call.”

Koba Ryckewaert contributed reporting.

item.title: A 31,000-Mile Walk Ends in England, at Mom’s House
item.description:
Where does a 31,000-mile walk end?

For Karl Bushby, it was his mother’s house in Hull, a port city on the east coast of England. He had walked around the globe for 28 years.

Mr. Bushby, 56, spoke to a crowd in the city center on Monday before he strolled the final miles to see his mother, Angela Bushby, who had decorated her yard with Union Jack bunting and a banner welcoming her boy.

It had been decades since Mr. Bushby was in his hometown. He began his walk in Punta Arenas, Chile, in November 1998, heading north to the Bering Strait, which he crossed on foot in March 2006. He continued across Asia and Europe.

Along the way, he traversed some of the world’s harshest landscapes, like the jungle of the Darién Gap. He was arrested and deported, and he got lost.

He had self-imposed rules for the walk, which included that he would not set foot in Britain until his journey concluded. This made it difficult to see his son, and his son’s daughter. She is 12, and Mr. Bushby had not met her before Monday.

Another rule was that Mr. Bushby would not use a mode of transport, like a car, a boat or a plane, to travel. So, in order to conclude his journey, he had to swim across the English Channel in October.

He made it to England, and arrived Monday in Hull with his main companion: a modified golf trolley that he has used to haul camping supplies, clothing, toiletries, food and water.

The documentarian Werner Herzog was there to welcome Mr. Bushby and his trolley. Last week, Mr. Bushby said on social media that Mr. Herzog would be making a documentary about him.

At a news conference on Monday, Mr. Bushby said he would be kept busy for the next year with the documentary and a book he is planning to write.

First, though, he had to process what it meant to be back in Hull.

“It’s difficult to explain how all that felt today,” Mr. Bushby said. “It’s all still one great big, blurry mess at the moment in my head.”

item.title: America Votes
item.description:
It’s Election Day in the United States, and the whole world seems to be remarkably engaged. I found myself discussing with a Welsh dentist the chances that Kansas will elect a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932. An Indian friend had a lot to say about Elon Musk spending nearly half a billion dollars to boost Republican candidates.

And of course everyone wants to know the outcome. Most polls show Democrats with a sizable lead, though polls have been wrong before. What would a big Democratic win mean for President Trump’s last two years in power? If his party loses, will he accept the outcome? The fact that this question now routinely hangs over elections in the U.S. is, in itself, amazing.

Last week, we asked you to send us your questions on the midterms, which are held halfway through a president’s term. You sent many, so thank you. We selected five and asked our colleagues who’ve been reporting on the elections to respond.

What, realistically, could a Democrat-led Congress do to restrain Trump? — Keith Parr, France

Annie Karni, congressional correspondent:

If Democrats win back the House — the lower chamber of Congress — they will have subpoena power and will be conducting oversight and investigations into the administration. And they will have to consider whether it is worth their time and the political price that may come with moving forward with impeachment against cabinet officials, or the president himself. If they win back the Senate — the upper chamber — Democrats would also have the power to block any Trump cabinet appointments or judicial nominees.

They will also be in control of what bills come to the floor. And many Democrats think that some of the popular legislation they plan to bring up if they win the majority — like reinstating subsidies for people who buy the health insurance known as Obamacare — could attract some Republican support in the Senate. And even if Trump refuses to sign it, they see a political upside in forcing him to veto broadly popular legislation.

Can the federal government actually overturn results that they don’t like? — Elena Yee, United States

Devlin Barrett, who covers the U.S. Justice Department:

No. The Constitution gives the authority to administer elections to the states, not the federal government.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the administration won’t try to influence the outcome. In 2020, Trump urged state election officials in Georgia to “find” roughly 11,000 more votes to change the outcome there. That effort failed. This year, the administration has filed aggressive lawsuits seeking to assert greater control over the elections. To date, those suits have been resoundingly unsuccessful; most election experts and lawyers expect the administration’s ongoing legal gambits to continue to fail, even if they reach the Supreme Court.

The Constitution also does not grant the president sweeping emergency powers to affect elections. And there are laws on the books designed to ensure access to the polls and to explicitly bar armed federal agents from being present at polling stations.

Whatever the outcome, will it have any effect on tariffs and the Iran war? — Samarkant Kukreja, India

David Sanger, White House and national security correspondent:

Trump has enormous latitude when it comes to tariffs, no matter who controls Congress. And he has powers as commander in chief that mean he could keep forces in and around the Persian Gulf without Congress having much say.

But the fact is that the tariff policy hasn’t been very effective. And Trump himself has backed off somewhat, notably when he placed huge tariffs on Chinese imports and Beijing shot back by shutting off shipments of rare earths and magnets.

On the conflict with Iran, it’s more complicated. The House passed, and the Senate rejected (by a single vote), an effort to invoke the War Powers Resolution and require the president to pull American troops out of the region. He would have vetoed it, and there were not enough votes to override, so the vote was mostly symbolic. And that is unlikely to change.

But it’s notable that Congress has never approved the White House request for supplemental funds to pay for the Iran action. So at some point, it’s possible that Trump could run out of money for the war, meaning he would probably look for ways to move other funds to accomplish his goals.

Money talks loudly in U.S. politics. If Democrats win the midterms, is there any appetite to change this? — Andrew Levens, Britain

Theodore Schleifer, who covers money in politics:

No. I have been writing about this topic for a decade now, and each successive year I become increasingly convinced that the Democratic Party is equally bought-in on the status quo. In some ways, the left has leapfrogged the right in finding more creative ways to use big money in the political system, such as soliciting money through organizations that do not disclose their donors. The Democratic Party’s voters might say they want to see less money in politics, but the actual incumbent politicians are often advantaged by the current system, given how skilled the party has gotten at courting big donors. And so I do not think there is enough momentum to actually force change.

How likely is it that a Democratic win could signal success for Democrats in the presidential race? — Ilias Papounidis, the Netherlands

Lisa Lerer, national political correspondent:

A Democratic sweep in the 2026 midterms would indicate that voters are willing to give the party another look. But it’s far from a sign of certain victory in 2028.

Traditionally, midterm elections act as referendums on a president’s first two years in office. These races are no exception. Much of the Democratic strength appears to stem from deep unhappiness with President Trump. Majorities say they disapprove of some of his signature policies, including the Iran war, tariffs and aggressive immigration enforcement.

There are some bright signs for Democrats. Their candidates appear to be winning back Latino voters and young men, who swung to Trump in 2024.

But voters aren’t giving particularly high marks to the Democratic Party. Surveys indicate that there is still dissatisfaction with the party’s national brand. And some of the most successful Democratic candidates are working hard to distance themselves from Democratic leaders in Washington. So, even if their candidates win, Democrats still have plenty of work to do to persuade Americans to send them back into the White House.

Ultrawealthy donors: The biggest U.S. donors have spent $2 billion in the midterm elections.

Cost of living: Concerns about high prices have dominated the race, with many voters linking Trump’s policies with inflation.

The presidential weave: An A.I.-assisted review of Trump’s public statements found that he is more vulgar, uninhibited and incoherent than a decade ago.

The Vatican owns no dedicated planes and has no equivalent to Air Force One, the plane that carries the American president. Instead, the pope always flies business class on charter flights operated by regular airlines. For more than six decades, ITA Airways (and its predecessor Alitalia) has been the Vatican’s preferred airline for the first leg of the pope’s foreign journeys.

Flights with the Holy Father aboard, however, are not ordinary flights. For one, they’re almost always on time, unlike over half of ITA’s other flights last year.

Leading the crew on more than 80 of those flights is Gennaro Anastasio, a senior cabin manager. Anastasio is preparing for the pope’s trip to Latin America, which is set to start on Friday. Read more about what happens on a papal plane.

Korean words or slightly altered versions of them are increasingly being heard in conversations between young Japanese. Moeka Takamatsu, a student in Tokyo, said she often used Korean words like jinjja (really) and mianhae (sorry).

The phenomenon is called Hanbono, a portmanteau of the words Hanguko (Korean) and Ilbono (Japanese). During the Japanese colonial era, Koreans were pressured to adopt the Japanese language. Now the Korean language is seeping into Japan’s youth culture, thanks to the success of K-pop, K-dramas and world-renowned beauty products. Read more about Hanbono.

item.title: Stranded ‘Endless Cruise’ Ship May Be Headed for the Auction Block
item.description:
Stranded cruise passengers’ efforts to cobble together enough funding to salvage their multiyear voyage appear to have faltered on Monday. The ship, the Odyssey, now in Cambodia, appears likely to be auctioned.

Last week, after two years at sea, the cruise ground to a sudden halt in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, when the ship’s operator, Villa Vie Residences, announced it could no longer afford fuel. The 200 passengers, who had paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the residential cruise, disembarked and have spent the past week trying to retrieve their belongings from the ship while planning what comes next.

An effort by several passengers to buy the ship failed to come together over the weekend. The lender and the ship-management team from the Columbia Group are preparing to take control of the ship and plan to sell it at auction.

“Villa Vie is still technically in possession, but the bank is taking control and will start the 60-90 day process of securing their collateral,” Villa Vie’s founder, Mikael Petterson, told The New York Times via text message. “We hope to have a restructure completed much sooner.”

When the sailing was suspended last week, Villa Vie said that it was because of “extraordinary increases in fuel costs” caused by the war with Iran and that the company was working to restructure and recapitalize over the next 60 days.

Unlike short-term vacation cruises, Villa Vie marketed its multiyear voyage as an affordable “home at sea” for retirees and remote workers, with extended port calls for deeper cultural immersion. Prices ranged from about $120,000 to $440,000, in addition to fixed monthly fees of $3,500 to $11,000.

Some passengers said they would keep traveling in Asia, while others have decided to stay in Cambodia while they await news of what will happen to the ship, holding out hope that the trip of a lifetime isn’t over.

Joel Greiff, a 57-year-old former hospitality worker, was battling severe stress and undergoing radiation treatment for an amyloid protein buildup when he decided to change his life. He sold his condo in Naples, Fla., and took an early withdrawal from his 401(k), paying $350,000 for Villa Vie’s Endless Horizons program, which promised him permanent residency for the life of the ship with no monthly fees.

He boarded the Odyssey on Oct. 1 and spent only 26 days on board before all the passengers were told to get off.

“The ship has been in trouble for months, and I think I had already come to terms with the reality that I might lose my money when I got on,” Mr. Greiff said. As a Plan B, he said he would help other residents get back on their feet and then live in Asia, where he said he could have “wonderful experiences.”

This wasn’t the first time the Odyssey had run into money trouble. In late July, when the ship was docked in Singapore, the operators ran out of money and made emergency cash calls to residents to cover fuel and operational costs and help prevent the ship from being impounded, according to communications on an internal app called Circle that were reviewed by The Times. To save the ship, the operators started a program that offered guests the opportunity to buy more cabins and benefits at discounted rates.

The residents said they raised $400,000 for fuel to leave Singapore and paid it out of one passenger’s personal bank account to avoid sending any more money to the ship’s operators.

In another effort to save the cruise, three of the passengers started a resident-backed investment company to buy and assume operating control of the ship. That initiative collapsed over the weekend after the residents failed to reach an agreement with the lender and realized, after reviewing Villa Vie’s financial records, that the ship had more debt than they had expected.

While the operators said they were still looking for investors to salvage the cruise, most residents said they were financially tapped out.

Cherie Ohlsson, 77, a genealogist who sold her home in Florida before embarking on the cruise, said she spent almost $1.5 million on her cabin and various payments to try to save the voyage but had nothing left to give.

“It was magical,” she said, “to be surrounded by water all the time and travel the world effortlessly with wonderful people who became family. There’s nothing like it.”

She said she did not know what would come next and was staying in a hotel in Cambodia, taking each day hour by hour: “I’m just not ready for it to end.”

item.title: A Canadian Sketch Show Beats American Late Night to the Punchline
item.description:
Hours after Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary five days into the job, the Canadian satirical series “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” captured the chaos in a sketch posted online — beating American late-night comedy shows to the punchline.

Some 48 hours later, and a week before the rapper Nicki Minaj traveled on Air Force One to rally for President Trump in Michigan, “22 Minutes” imagined the MAGA darling as Ms. Zacharia’s successor.

In both cases, the creative team on the show, Canada’s version of “Saturday Night Live,” did not wait for their weekly broadcast. The polished sketches went straight to the show’s TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, attracting nearly 24 million views.

For the last 34 years, this sketch comedy show has reliably roasted Canadian and American politics, culture and quirks. But “22 Minutes” is having a renaissance buoyed by Mr. Trump — in particular his trade war, tariffs, threats and insults toward Canada. Television audiences are up, and social media viewership is growing rapidly.

“Social media has opened up our show beyond what I thought was capable,” said Stacey McGunnigle, a cast member and writer who has created and portrayed many MAGA women, most memorably Karoline Leavitt, Natalie Harp and, ever so briefly, Ms. Zacharias.

“The show’s been on a long time, and we can be the butt of the joke sometimes as far as what people think our demographic is,” she said. “But in the six seasons I’ve been here, more young people are coming up to us who love it and watch it all the time.”

The characters Ms. McGunnigle most likes to play are pro-life, pro-gun, pro-war and pro-push-up bra. “Too much makeup, no moral compass, a pathological desire to protect the patriarchy, and blonde. Terrifying!” she said.

The show, which airs Tuesday nights on the publicly funded Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, leans progressive but traffics in nonpartisan political satire — anyone in the headlines is fair game. Since Mr. Trump began his second term, the show routinely points its lens at the United States and its deteriorating relationship with Canada.

“This Hour Has 22 Minutes” is the nosy neighbor with permanently raised eyebrows.

Fans include Graydon Carter, the Canadian-born former editor of Vanity Fair and co-founder of Spy magazine.

“Canadians are feeling an uncharacteristic blush of patriotism,” he said. “And there’s nothing like friction and impending chaos to bring out the satirists.”

Ms. McGunnigle operates with fast-twitch newsroom instincts. As soon as Ms. Zacharia held her first disastrous White House briefing, she knew the show had to do something. “And that 14-minute press conference,” Ms. McGunnigle said. “I felt we weren’t going to have her for long.”

While they were shooting the piece a few days later, Ms. Zacharia was fired. Ms. McGunnigle immediately began improvising, turning a sketch about Ms. Zacharia’s disastrous first news conference into one about her last. A bonus: “Saturday Night Live” was dark that week.

“Stacey McGunnigle’s Katie Zacharia was superb,” Mr. Carter said. “But for her it was a bit like getting the coveted lead in a play that closes on opening night.”

The weekly broadcast averages 571,000 viewers, up 31 percent from 435,000 last season, with 25- to 54-year-olds the leading demographic. The “Meet Katie” sketch has more than 21.5 million views across social media, and the first Leavitt sketch more than 7.8 million.

Mark Critch, a veteran cast member and writer in his 24th season, plays Mr. Trump.

“We’re the quiet house next door, and the house on the other side of the fence, they have a lot of loud parties, and there’s always arguing in the yard,” he said. “We’re watching over the fence going, ‘Oh, my God, what’s going on?’ We get to observe, which is a good thing for comedy.”

Mr. Critch has taken his Trump to Greenland. He whipped up a “Quiet, Piggy” sketch after the president insulted a reporter with the phrase. As Mr. Trump, he fulminated over The New York Times’s exclusive interview with Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a cold open. In an attempt to rekindle Canada-U.S. relations Mr. Critch, as himself, met with Gov. Janet Mills of Maine, who implored him to ask Canadians to resume visiting her state.

“I mean God almighty,” he said, “Even with all the arguing that goes on, there’s nothing a Canadian gets excited about more than American attention.”

Drawing inspiration from the Trump administration isn’t entirely new for the show. What is more recent is the speed at which the show reacts to news. Without social media, the show, taped on Mondays, would struggle to stay timely on Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States.

“TV shows are big machines and you don’t want to be late to the party,” Mr. Critch said. “There’s another audience that we can get to right away. When something happens in the moment, now the whole building pivots.”

Mike Allison, the executive producer and showrunner, said more people tuned in as Canadian-U.S. tensions escalated. Especially amusing has been the opportunity for interplay between Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney, played by Mark McKinney, on the war in Iran, reverse psychology, and McDonald’s. But not every sketch needs a Canadian tie.

“When writers pitch Kristi Noem or Kash Patel, that’s us looking over the fence at all the crazy characters running the country,” Mr. Allison said. “But U.S. politics have become Canadian politics.”

“22 Minutes has the DNA of the knowing outsider,” Mr. Carter said.

It always has. Twenty-five years ago, “Talking to Americans” was a popular segment testing how little Americans knew about Canada. Highlights included a Columbia University professor agreeing that the government should stop putting senior citizens on ice floes to die, and Mike Huckabee, then the governor of Arkansas, congratulating Canada on preserving its national igloo.

Mr. Critch often hears from Americans who don’t realize the show is Canadian.

“They will say, ‘Oh, good, thank you. That’s what I feel.’ But then you’ll get some saying, ‘You don’t know anything! That’s our president! Shut up!’” he said. “Something I see that’s actually very Canadian is Americans saying they’re sorry. ‘I’m so sorry this is happening. I’m so sorry they’re saying these things about your country. We love Canadians.’”

item.title: China’s Message to Its Rivals: You Need What We Make
item.description:
They are among the biggest machines in the world: steel cylinders, some as long as a football field, armed with rotating discs that can chew through rock to clear the way for roads and railways. Known as tunnel boring machines, they are made by only a handful of companies, mostly in factories in China.

India uses them to dig tunnels, including in the Himalayas, to improve its ability to send troops to defend its contested border with China. But starting next month, Beijing is likely to be able to control whether India gets to buy them.

The machines are part of a broader effort by China to control what leaves Chinese factories and laboratories for foreign lands. In the past month, Beijing has moved to control the exports of dozens of technologies, including drones, artificial intelligence models and agents, and certain processes used to develop advanced medicines and to make solar panels.

The overall push could make it much harder for companies in the United States and elsewhere to set up solar energy equipment factories that would compete against Chinese manufacturers. And it could soon make it more difficult for anyone outside China to gain access to the latest and most powerful Chinese A.I. models.

The planned restrictions show that Beijing is doubling down on its strategy of making Chinese factories indispensable to the world, even as many governments are alarmed by their countries’ dependence on China and are pushing to be less reliant.

In the United States, concern over China’s grip on rare earths has spurred the government to revive the country’s own mining and processing industry for the minerals. In Europe, Japan and elsewhere, governments are trying to reclaim their ability to make antibiotics and active ingredients of medicines, many of which now come from China. In India, the transport minister has urged companies to make tunnel boring machines locally.

For Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, the controls are the realization of a plan he laid out years ago, when the pandemic exposed China’s dependence on foreign countries for advanced medical equipment like ventilators and life-support systems, as well as for raw materials and specialized parts.

He declared that China would develop “trump card” technologies in industries such as high-speed trains, renewable energy and telecommunications. That would make China not only more self-sufficient, but deter countries from trying to cut China off.

Mr. Xi has depicted China as locked in a long struggle with the West, which he sees as trying to contain China’s rise.

Beijing needs leverage to ensure that China can still get what it needs from other countries — namely their customers and advanced technologies like jet engines and high-end chips, said Kirsten Asdal, a founder of Asdal Advisory, a consultancy that focuses on Chinese political research.

“Xi and the party see themselves as naturally embattled” against the West, she said, and have been “angling for a confrontation sooner or later, whenever the opportunity and capability present itself.”

At home, the Communist Party has framed China’s push for industrial and technological might as a fight for survival, echoing the struggles of the party’s revolutionary past.

In recent days, the party has repeatedly invoked the Long March, the Red Army’s epic 6,000-mile strategic retreat that cemented Mao Zedong’s leadership and became its defining myth of triumph over impossible odds. By drawing on that history, the party may be trying to reassure ordinary Chinese that endurance under its leadership will carry China through a time of slower economic growth, a prolonged housing crisis and growing hostility abroad.

In a recent front-page editorial commemorating the 90th anniversary of the Long March, People’s Daily, the party’s mouthpiece, called for the country to “focus on the ‘chokehold’ key core technologies” and “stiffen the Chinese backbone” of self-reliance.

In a clear reference to the United States, the editorial praised China for weathering tariffs and trade wars and urged readers to prepare for a “great struggle.” The call to secure technological choke points was also likened to the way the Red Army took the “strategic initiative” on the battlefield to ultimately defeat the Nationalists.

China has said that the recent flurry of export controls and proposed rules are needed to protect Chinese business interests. The country has spent decades and billions of dollars developing its dominance of the manufacturing of solar equipment, for instance, and it argues that it must restrict the export of core equipment to prevent competitors from trying to replicate China’s supply chain domestically.

China has also said that more controls are needed to guard against threats to national security.

“China is beginning to more systematically consider which technologies and equipment can be exported, to whom they should be sold and what their ultimate applications will be,” said Sun Chenghao, a foreign relations expert at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

He said, for instance, that the risks that A.I. could be used for cyberattacks or that machines that bore tunnels and that dredge mud could be used by militaries against China are legitimate reasons for Beijing to vet where these technologies go.

The proposed controls may also be a part of tit-for-tat actions that China and the United States have traded in recent months, despite a broader trade truce. The Trump administration added BGI, a major Chinese genomics company to a trade blacklist aimed at barring products made with forced labor in China. Earlier, the Treasury Department proposed regulations prohibiting U.S. companies and investors from taking investment stakes in Chinese biotechnology firms.

President Trump and Mr. Xi are expected to meet in China later this month and next month in Miami.

American restrictions and sanctions on China helped teach Beijing that great powers need economic weapons as much as they need aircraft carriers and long-range missiles, some analysts have said. Washington first cut two of China’s largest technology companies, Huawei and ZTE, off from American chips and software, then restricted exports of advanced chips to China broadly, curbs that continue to hurt China’s A.I. ambitions.

During its trade war with the second Trump administration, Beijing choked off exports to the United States of rare earths, the minerals needed to make fighter jets, cars and everyday technologies. That pressured Washington into a truce.

Some Chinese analysts worry that Beijing’s rare earths strategy has been too successful. The United States and many of its allies and partners are now scrambling to develop alternative sources.

Part of this month’s flood of Chinese controls was aimed at establishing new points of leverage.

“China is concerned that it might lose its ‘rare earths card,’” said Zhao Minghao, an international relations scholar at Fudan University in Shanghai. “So, what other cards does China still hold? How can China effectively counter U.S. sanctions or tariff measures? I believe Beijing is prioritizing this highly at the present.”

China’s single-minded focus on technological self-sufficiency carries risks for Beijing.

Economists have long urged Beijing to invest in pensions, health care and unemployment benefits so that residents feel secure enough to spend.

“That obsession with developing technology and protecting it is leading to a massive misallocation of resources in China that is generating slower growth and higher debt,” said Scott Kennedy, a researcher on the Chinese economy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

The new controls could also alarm other trading partners like Europe, which is already uneasy about a flood of cheap Chinese exports.

“That kind of business by threat is not going to be something that is sustainable,” Mr. Kennedy said.

Even some Chinese analysts acknowledge the danger.

“If uncertainty becomes too high, customers may seek alternatives,” Mr. Sun of Tsinghua said.

That is already happening in India. Experts say that China had been holding up exports of tunnel boring machines as early as 2024, before it added them to its list of export controls. As a result, India has had to seek out other suppliers.

Yet New Delhi had few ways to retaliate because its economic ties with China were so thin, said Pranay Kotasthane, chair of the High Tech Geopolitics Program at the Takshashila Institution in Bengaluru, India.

“China is indiscriminately expanding the scope of their export controls to include basic equipment that aren’t even strategic,” he added. “They are demonstrating that in any political conflict, they can counter with industrial leverage.”

item.title: Up in the Clouds With the Pope, It’s Still Commercial
item.description:
A day before Pope Leo XIV departed for France in September, on the fourth major international trip of his papacy, the crew of the plane he was to use, known colloquially as “Shepherd One,” gathered to learn the inviolable rules of the flight.

No selfies with the pope, said Gennaro Anastasio, the senior cabin manager, as he reeled off a list of dos and don’ts.

If the Holy Father offers his hand, shake it, don’t kiss it. Make no personal requests of the pontiff, such as asking that he pray for family members. Check the bathroom at the front of the plane — the one used by the pope — several times throughout the flight and keep it spotless. Don’t speak directly to the pope, but talk to his personal secretaries.

And mind your language. The men wearing black robes with red sashes and skullcaps should be addressed as “eminenza,” the salutation for cardinals, the highest-ranking clergy except for the pope. The men in purple caps and sashes are bishops and should be greeted as “eccellenza.”

“Don’t mess up,” said Mr. Anastasio, an impish 67-year-old. “If, though, you call a bishop ‘eminenza,’ he’ll say, ‘No I’m not an eminenza,’” he added with a chuckle. “And you can say, ‘You’ll become one!’”

Above all, he said, the crew should deliver anything the papal passengers ask for. “There’s never the need to say, ‘I’m sorry, it’s not possible, that’s not allowed, it can’t be done,’” Mr. Anastasio said. “Here, it’s done. Always.”

The Vatican, unlike the United States government, owns no dedicated planes and has no equivalent to Air Force One. Instead, the pope always flies commercial — in business class on charter flights operated by regular airlines.

For more than six decades, ITA Airways — and its predecessor, Alitalia — has been the preferred airline for the first leg of the pope’s foreign journeys, and sometimes more. Mr. Anastasio has led crews on more than 80 of those flights, but many members of those crews do it only once. Mr. Anastasio is preparing for the pope’s trip to Latin America, a 12-day journey through three countries starting Friday.

Last month, Pope Leo underwent surgery for lung cancer, but his doctors have cleared him to travel.

For ITA, being the pope’s preferred carrier is a clear bragging right. The pope’s international trips are among the most public events of any papacy, allowing the pontiff to meet with the faithful in their home countries and demonstrate the reach of the Roman Catholic Church.

Joerg Eberhart, ITA’s chief executive, said the role was not guaranteed. The airline regularly competes in Vatican tenders for the main papal flights, he said, and the airline loses money operating them.

These are no ordinary flights. For starters, they are almost always perfectly on time, unlike over half of ITA’s other flights last year. The papal plane’s call sign — AZ4000 — is instantly recognizable to air traffic control towers across the world, allowing them to clear routes to ensure the flights take off and land according to schedule.

That means the plane can push back and head for the runway as soon as the pope steps aboard and sits in his usual front-row seat on the left side of the plane.

The typical limits for carry-on baggage are overlooked. During the taxi to the runway, the cabin crew skips the usual announcements and safety videos to allow the Vatican news corps to work without background noise. All the seat backs — including in economy class, where the journalists sit — are topped by a small cloth, known as an antimacassar, that is embroidered with the pope’s coat of arms. (They make for nice souvenirs.)

In Rome, the planes take off from a terminal reserved for V.I.P. charter flights at Fiumicino Airport. Officers from Italy’s military police force and the Swiss Guard, the Vatican security service, patrol the aisles. Bishops and cardinals are driven directly to the tarmac and board shortly before the pope, who arrives by black car or papal helicopter just before takeoff and climbs the staircase to the front door, news cameras flashing.

On rare occasions, the papal flights cannot be cleared for on-time takeoff. When Leo’s predecessor, Pope Francis, was departing for Cuba in 2015, another jet stalled on the runway, Mr. Anastasio recalled. Francis suggested the pilot simply fly over the beached plane, and Mr. Anastasio had to explain that was not possible, he said. The flight departed 63 minutes late, but the pilot made up the lost time in the air so that Francis still made his first appointment in Havana.

Mishaps can arise on arrival, too.

When Pope Leo landed in Cameroon in April, Mr. Anastasio noticed that a ruby-red carpet with gold trim, laid out by local officials on the passenger staircase, was twisted in places. Mr. Anastasio ran down to straighten it to ensure the pope would not trip, he said.

Perhaps the most important detail for any flight is getting the onboard meals right. On a recent trip to France, Mr. Anastasio said, he needed to figure out how to cram in a breakfast service around the pope’s traditional one-on-one greetings with journalists on a flight lasting less than two hours.

He calculated that the crew would have no more than 30 minutes to get from the front of the cabin to the back, which meant that the passengers would need a meal that they could scarf in 10 minutes or less.

After consulting with ITA’s chefs, the Vatican opted for a tray with a scrambled-egg-and-bacon sandwich, slices of prosciutto, pecorino and primo sale cheese, fruit, petit fours, a twisted roll and a croissant.

For many journalists, it’s a rare chance to experience business-class service with meals served on ceramic plates with cloth napkins, drinks served in real glass, cutlery made from silverware and a menu printed on a thick card.

Mr. Anastasio said he liked to add local touches for meals — hence the croissants for France and the Turkish chocolates he bought in Istanbul to serve in gift boxes on the return flight.

During the eras of John Paul II and Benedict XVI, Mr. Anastasio said, the popes and their entourages ate premium meals while journalists and lay staff from the Vatican ate economy-class fare.

Then Francis boarded a papal flight, observed the formal meal service for the clergy — and asked Mr. Anastasio what the journalists ate. When the cabin manager showed the pope the economy-class trays, Francis told him, “I am not a king,” Mr. Anastasio recalled. From then on, the journalists ate the same meals as clergy.

Mr. Anastasio, nevertheless, made sure to offer some special treats to Francis. Once he learned the pope liked Havanna lemon cookies from Argentina, Mr. Anastasio started bringing the biscuits on every flight. And Francis occasionally asked for customized meals, including rice with Parmigiano-Reggiano and Amalfi lemons that Mr. Anastasio personally prepared on board.

Benedict once asked for some premium mortadella — sliced pork sausage — from Campotosto in central Italy, recalled Giovanni Bernardi, a chef for ITA’s main meal supplier. Mr. Anastasio joked that the meal almost caused “a diplomatic incident” because the flight was on its way to a Muslim country that he would not name.

And what about Leo? Mr. Anastasio said the new pope has made no special requests so far.

“He’s really simple,” he said.

Josephine de La Bruyère contributed reporting.

I have now traveled three times with Pope Leo on major international trips. Flying with the pope is a unique experience, and in some ways rather more prosaic than one would expect. The planes are simply chartered commercial jets, with the same layouts you might find on any international flight. (Not a lot of legroom or elbow room at the back.) But there are protocols and rituals, and it was fun to learn from the inside what the crew is expected to do when up in the air with the leader of the Roman Catholic Church.

item.title: King Charles Meets Both Joy and Criticism on Caribbean Tour
item.description:
More than 100 residents of the South American nation of Guyana lined up outside an Indigenous cultural site on Friday, eager for a glimpse of King Charles III, the figurehead of a British state that ruled here until independence almost 60 years ago. Some brought their small children.

Standing nearby in the searing sun, about two dozen protesters waved signs demanding that Britain pay reparations and apologize for the millions of enslaved Africans who were trafficked across the Atlantic in the 1700s and 1800s. They chanted loudly: “Not our king!”

As Charles makes a seven-day visit to three of Britain’s former colonies, his country’s history of slavery — and what he and the British government should say or do about it — continues to divide opinion across the once-sprawling empire.

“They bought slaves, sold slaves and made money from slavery and then paid the slave owners millions of dollars and the slaves and their descendants got nothing,” said Elton Campbell, referring to British legislation passed in the 1830s that compensated slave owners for the freeing of slaves after the country outlawed the practice.

Mr. Campbell, a 76-year-old insurance agent in Guyana’s capital, added, “Let the king explain that to the nation and our Black people around the world.”

For the first time on Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain said the government was open to offering a formal apology for the country’s role in the slave trade, which he described as “brutal and barbaric.”

But he rejected demands to pay reparations to the descendants of slaves, writing in an opinion article: “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

Mr. Burnham and the king are both scheduled to address leaders of the Commonwealth at a gathering in Antigua on Tuesday, though it is not clear what they will say. At the start of his Caribbean tour, Charles said that “it is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past, in these islands and beyond.”

In the Bahamas, where the king’s events included dancing in a carnival parade known as the Junkanoo, some residents warmly welcomed his role as their country’s official head of state.

“Whatever you feel about the royals personally, we are still members of the Commonwealth,” said Margaret Ramsingh, 52, referring to the voluntary organization of 56 nations, most of which were former British colonies.

“I understand what people are saying about reparations,” Ms. Ramsingh said in an interview last week, “but at some point in time we have to move forward.”

During his trip, the king has not tried to dodge the issue of what he has called a “dark stain” on Britain’s past. In Guyana on Friday, he visited the site of the Demerara Slave Rebellion of 1823, where colonial forces brutally crushed a rebellion by thousands of enslaved men and women, killing hundreds.

If Buckingham Palace officials had hoped that some of his seven-day trip could also be focused on issues like climate change and nature conservation — issues that have long been priorities for the king — they may have been disappointed by the persistent conversations about reparations.

Just hours before Charles met with Mohammed Ifraan Ali, the president of Guyana, on Thursday, Mr. Ali said in an interview that an apology for slavery would be “the next step” to be taken. Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said Saturday that Mr. Burnham’s openness to an apology was welcomed. But she did not back away from demands for reparations.

“On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she wrote in a statement.

Interviews with residents of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua revealed an eagerness to discuss the topic of the British slave trade, the monarchy and the government’s role in making amends for Britain’s history.

Daren Matthew Ward, 51, an insurance manager in Antigua, said the king’s visit to the island was a positive thing and could help bring much-needed investment to the country. But he said the discussions about the legacy of slavery are important.

“Nobody present is, you know, guilty of or complicit in the crime that took place many years ago,” Mr. Ward said. “On our end, we’re saying there are certain historical disadvantages that are inherent in our societies as a result of what happened during the slave trade. And those injustices and imbalances need to be addressed in some way.”

Others in the country of just under 100,000 people were more blunt about what they expect from their monarch.

“At the end of the day, why are we trying to impress our former slave masters?” asked St. Claire Henry, 39, an IT technician in Antigua. “These are not people that genuinely cared for us. He acknowledged that grave things were done in the past. OK, acknowledge it. Say sorry, do something. Pay us something.”

At the king’s first stop in the Bahamas, the king delivered a speech at a youth rally, in front of bleachers filled with young schoolchildren cheering wildly for the monarch.

And at Parliament Square in Nassau, the streets were lined with more than 1,000 people, many of them holding their iPhones up high to snap a royal photo. The mood at the event was joyous and excited, with little evidence of protesters demanding an apology or reparations from the king.

But such carefully produced events rarely capture the full range of opinions, especially on sensitive topics like slavery.

Endal Adderley, 56, a retired secondary school principal on Long Island in the Bahamas, said it is the British government that should take responsibility for slavery.

“The Black people who were disenfranchised, who had lost all they had, even lost their names, their languages, they came over, they survived, they built communities, they built societies, they now are building nations,” Mr. Adderley said. “All they’re asking for is some justice and some economic reparations in cash or in kind, and I fully endorse that.”

He added: “In the Caribbean, I don’t see any reason for us to be bowing down to a king anymore.”

Joy Burrows, 70, is a part of the generation in the Bahamas that remembers a time when the Union Jack flew over the archipelago and schoolchildren sang “God Save the Queen.” She said she believes the Bahamas has moved on and there is no need to address what has already happened.

“I think that this is a part of history,” she said, “and we can’t change history or what has happened.”

item.title: Israel Turns to Next Big Question: Who Gets a Shot at Being Prime Minister?
item.description:
This week, Israeli party leaders will trickle into the residence of President Isaac Herzog to officially recommend their pick for Israel’s next prime minister following the inconclusive election last Tuesday.

In two days of livestreamed meetings set to begin on Wednesday, politicians from 11 parties, including those representing secular liberals, ultra-Orthodox Jews and Arab voters, will make their case to Mr. Herzog. He will then bestow the mandate to build a coalition on whichever candidate he deems the most viable, who will have up to six weeks to form a government.

Most party leaders are expected to back either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the longtime right-wing leader, or his main rival, the center-right politician Gadi Eisenkot. Neither man’s party won a clear 61-seat majority in balloting for the 120-member Parliament, most likely meaning that weeks or months of negotiations among the parties and elected lawmakers lie ahead.

Behind the scenes, politicians are weighing the path forward and wrangling for the upper hand. With no one having emerged from the election with a decisive victory, Mr. Netanyahu, Mr. Eisenkot and the rest are left to cajole and squeeze opponents and would-be allies alike.

“It’s a game of chicken,” said Nevo Cohen, a political strategist who ran the 2022 election campaign for the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Mr. Netanyahu has long exercised a tight grip over his bloc of conservative and religious parties. But some could always bolt — potentially, ultra-Orthodox or more moderate right-wingers in his own Likud faction — in exchange for influence in an Eisenkot-led government, political analysts said.

Mr. Eisenkot could also look to form a government by relying on Arab parties that have long sat on the sidelines of Israeli politics, or by partnering with Mr. Netanyahu to form a unity government. Either option would be tricky because some of his allies promised on the campaign trail never to work with Mr. Netanyahu, or with Arab lawmakers to form a government.

On Monday, Avigdor Liberman, a key figure in the opposition bloc, said he would recommend Mr. Eisenkot for prime minister. But he reiterated his longstanding vow not to share power with Mr. Netanyahu or serve in a minority government with Arab parties, further complicating matters for Mr. Eisenkot.

All the parties “are checking their internal situation to see how much room they have to maneuver,” said Lior Chorev, a political strategist who worked on former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s campaign, which picked up 12 seats in Parliament last week. “They want to know how far they can go.”

After the last election in 2022, Mr. Netanyahu swept to power with a 64-seat majority, allowing him to establish the most far-right government in Israel’s history. This time, the calculations are considerably more complex. Mr. Netanyahu and his allies’ majority dropped to 53 seats in Parliament, while Mr. Eisenkot’s opposition bloc garnered 48 seats.

Surging turnout among Israel’s Arab citizens also helped to deliver a historic result for the two main Arab-led parties — now potential kingmakers, with 19 seats between them — even as many Jewish Israelis reject the idea of a coalition government that includes them.

An Israeli opposition official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private negotiations, said that party leaders were feeling out one another’s red lines. These leaders were also drawing up legislative plans for when Israel’s Parliament, the Knesset, is sworn in this week, the official said.

While the coalition talks lurch onward, the Israeli opposition could take over the Parliament by appointing a new speaker. Mr. Eisenkot and his allies could then threaten to begin passing laws antithetical to Mr. Netanyahu and his coalition, turning up the pressure in the talks.

The coalition talks will be extraordinarily sensitive because if no one can make a government, Israel will head to yet another round of elections, said Izhar Shay, a former centrist lawmaker.

“The parties are negotiating — but in reality, they’re still campaigning, because this might turn into an election campaign in just a few months,” said Mr. Shay. “So they’re being cautious about what they say, because it could hurt them in elections which might be in four months, rather than four years.”

Mr. Netanyahu could have the most to gain from rolling the dice in a new election. As it stands, he remains prime minister until a new government can be formed, meaning he would stay in power for months if a new election were called. And political analysts say he could have better odds in a second round of voting.

That heaps pressure on Mr. Eisenkot to form a coalition.

Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s voters say that, despite their loathing for Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, joining with Mr. Netanyahu might make the most sense, as it would keep the ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties out of power. Such an arrangement is not without risk: Mr. Netanyahu has walked away from political agreements before when they no longer served him.

In 2020, a unity government between Mr. Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, a centrist opposition leader, collapsed after less than a year of power sharing. Under their coalition agreement, Mr. Netanyahu was supposed to yield the prime minister’s seat to Mr. Gantz, but instead he dissolved the Knesset and called new elections.

“We thought we were doing the right thing, and in the end Netanyahu cheated us,” said Mr. Shay, a lawmaker in Mr. Gantz’s party at the time.

Mr. Eisenkot’s other route is to form a minority government with the Arab parties, particularly the pragmatic Raam party, which got eight seats. The Joint List, which netted 11 seats, is unlikely to join his governing coalition, but it could block a no-confidence vote against the coalition in the Knesset, allowing him to form a minority government with fewer than 61 seats.

Joining forces with Arab parties has become a more difficult proposition since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel, which led to a rightward shift in the country’s politics. On Monday, Mr. Liberman — whose Yisrael Beiteinu party commands seven seats — declared that he would not join such a minority government, although he left the door open to other possibilities.

Further complicating matters, Mr. Netanyahu has accused Arab citizens of engaging in widespread electoral fraud and “stealing the election.” Israeli electoral officials have repeatedly said that there was no indication of systematic interference in the vote.

Analysts say Mr. Netanyahu’s racially charged campaign aims to further discredit any attempt by Mr. Eisenkot to engage Arab parties as partners.

“That’s the only scenario that Netanyahu is afraid of, so he’s trying to do things that will make a minority government impossible,” said Michael Koplow, an expert at the Israel Policy Forum, a research group.

An incident that surfaced Thursday gave Mr. Netanyahu an opening to cast doubt on the legitimacy of the high Arab vote.

Noam Sohlberg, the Supreme Court justice overseeing the country’s elections committee, said in a letter that he had seen intelligence indicating potential “improper influence through foreign funding” in the elections. He did not elaborate and said he “could not attest to the veracity of the suspicions.” He nevertheless sent a letter telling the head of Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to investigate.

The Likud party quickly issued a statement saying that the Arab parties had “stolen the elections in Israel.” The party incorrectly cited Mr. Sohlberg’s letter to Shin Bet, falsely saying it had reported that “foreign officials have bribed voters on behalf of the Arab parties.”

Three days later, Mr. Sohlberg issued a clarification, saying that there was no reason to “call into question the votes cast by Arab citizens.” But the claim that Arab parties had tainted the elections had already become a right-wing talking point, with the Likud saying that a “black cloud” hung over the vote.

On Wednesday, the Israeli Central Elections Committee is expected to meet to certify the official results by a vote. The far-right Jewish Power party, which is part of Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, has already said in a statement that it will refuse to do so, though it holds just two of the 34 votes in the committee’s general assembly.

Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting from Modiin, Israel.
